nodes.label: Continental System
nodes.full: The Continental System and Saint-Domingue’s loss push France to beet sugar, 1806–14.

nodes.label: Beet collapses in 1815
nodes.full: Forty French beet factories make 3.3 million lb in 1812, then collapse with peace.

nodes.label: Vilmorin’s beet
nodes.full: Vilmorin introduces a high-sucrose sugar beet in 1837.

nodes.label: Beet’s share
nodes.full: Beet is almost half the world’s sugar by 1880 and 59% by 1890.

nodes.label: Prices fall
nodes.full: Sugar prices fall to under a quarter of the 1840 level by 1900.

nodes.label: Quakers back beet
nodes.full: Early support for beet sugar comes from Quakers and abolitionists.

nodes.label: Slave trade banned
nodes.full: Britain and the US end the slave trade in 1807–08; Africans still go to Cuba and Brazil.

nodes.label: British emancipation
nodes.full: British slavery ends 1833–38, with apprenticeship and £20 million compensation.

nodes.label: Freed leave plantations
nodes.full: Freed people leave the plantations and farm small plots.

nodes.label: Indian indenture
nodes.full: Nearly 1.5 million Indians go out as indentured workers, 1834–1924.

nodes.label: Mauritius
nodes.full: Mauritius makes 9.4% of the world’s sugar by the mid-century, with Indian workers.

nodes.label: Natal
nodes.full: Natal’s cane grows with Indian workers from 1860.

nodes.label: Gandhi in Natal
nodes.full: Gandhi is radicalised in Natal’s sugar country.

nodes.label: Palmerston’s speech
nodes.full: Palmerston mocks Britain’s conscience over slave-grown sugar in 1841.

nodes.label: Duties abolished
nodes.full: Britain abolishes its sugar duties in 1846.

nodes.label: Cuba’s growth
nodes.full: Cuba grows from 19,000 to 446,000 tons in fifty years.

nodes.label: Africans to Cuba
nodes.full: More than 500,000 Africans land in Cuba after British abolition.

nodes.label: Ten Years’ War
nodes.full: Slaves walk off Cuba’s plantations in the war of 1868–78.

nodes.label: Cuban abolition
nodes.full: Cuba abolishes slavery in 1886, Brazil in 1888.

nodes.label: Chinese indenture
nodes.full: Over 150,000 indentured Chinese reach Cuba by 1873.

nodes.label: Cuba’s million tons
nodes.full: Cuba makes 750,000 tons in 1886 and over a million by 1900.

nodes.label: War of 1898
nodes.full: Sugar is ‘a decisive element’ in the road to the war of 1898.

nodes.label: Louisiana Purchase
nodes.full: The 1803 purchase opens the Mississippi delta to cane.

nodes.label: Louisiana’s estates
nodes.full: Louisiana has 75 mills in 1812 and 1,536 estates by 1861.

nodes.label: Louisiana’s Civil War
nodes.full: The Civil War cuts Louisiana’s plantations from 1,200 to 231.

nodes.label: Louisiana recovers
nodes.full: Louisiana recovers to 302,778 tons by 1900.

nodes.label: Kauai missionaries
nodes.full: Missionaries help the first Hawaiian sugar company in 1835.

nodes.label: Hawaii’s sugar
nodes.full: Hawaii goes from four tons in 1836 to 105,000 tons in 1886.

nodes.label: Reciprocity Treaty
nodes.full: The 1875–76 treaty gives Hawaii’s sugar the US market; Spreckels buys half the crop.

nodes.label: Japanese in Hawaii
nodes.full: Japanese contract workers arrive from 1865.

nodes.label: Hawaii’s depopulation
nodes.full: The Hawaiian population falls below 60,000 by the 1870s.

nodes.label: Planters’ constitution
nodes.full: Hawaii’s planters impose a constitution on the king in 1887.

nodes.label: Overthrow of 1893
nodes.full: US Marines help overthrow Hawaii’s queen in 1893.

nodes.label: Queensland
nodes.full: Queensland’s cane grows with Pacific island labour.

nodes.label: Blackbirding
nodes.full: Melanesians are taken to Queensland’s cane until 1904–06.

nodes.label: Vacuum pan
nodes.full: Howard patents the vacuum pan in 1813; it is standard by mid-century.

nodes.label: Steam mill
nodes.full: A steam-driven horizontal mill appears in 1816.

nodes.label: Centrifuge
nodes.full: The centrifuge cuts the time to dry sugar.

nodes.label: Refining standard
nodes.full: Acid, bone charcoal and the 95° Pol standard for refined sugar.

nodes.label: Steam in Cuba
nodes.full: Three steam mills in Cuba make six times what three ox mills do.

nodes.label: Suez and steamers
nodes.full: Steamers and Suez cut Asian sugar freight by up to 63%.

nodes.label: British refineries
nodes.full: 72 British refineries in 1864, 13 in 1913.

nodes.label: British consumption
nodes.full: British consumption rises from 18 lb in 1810 to 91 lb in 1914.

nodes.label: The poor’s sugar
nodes.full: Jam, bread and sweet tea feed Britain’s urban poor.

nodes.label: Keiller marmalade
nodes.full: Keiller starts marmalade in 1864.

nodes.label: Mason jar
nodes.full: The Mason jar of 1858 helps sugar preserve fruit.

nodes.label: US consumption
nodes.full: American consumption rises from 5 lb in 1788 to 80 lb in the 1890s.

nodes.label: Sugar Trust
nodes.full: Havemeyer’s Sugar Trust controls 98% of US refining in 1887.

nodes.label: McKinley Act
nodes.full: The 1890 McKinley Act changes the US sugar tariff.

nodes.label: US tariff
nodes.full: US sugar protection comes fully into force in 1842.

nodes.label: Soda fountains
nodes.full: Dr Pepper, Coca-Cola and Pepsi start in the South, 1885–98.

nodes.label: Quaker chocolate
nodes.full: Cadbury and Fry make drinking and eating chocolate from the 1830s on.

nodes.label: Graham’s warning
nodes.full: Sylvester Graham would ban refined sugar in 1839.

nodes.label: Guangdong and Taiwan
nodes.full: The Pearl River Delta gives up cane; only Taiwan modernises.

nodes.label: Population doubles
nodes.full: The world’s population almost doubles in the century.

edges: Smith and Walvin: the blockade pushed France to beet, and the factories of 1812 collapsed when peace came in 1815.
Smith: even after the collapse, Vilmorin’s breeding of 1837 revived the beet industry in several countries.
Smith: Vilmorin’s breeding and new extraction methods lowered costs, and beet grew to almost half of world sugar by 1880.
Mazumdar: subsidised beet and large cane stocks together drove the world price of sugar down.
Smith: Quakers and abolitionists gave early support to beet because they opposed slave-grown cane sugar.
Walvin: the British and US ban of 1807–08 left Cuba and Brazil taking Africans in unprecedented numbers.
Walvin: when emancipation came, large numbers of freed people left the plantations.
Walvin: planters and imperial governments, after ending slavery, turned to a new form of imported labour, from India.
In Mauritius 455,187 Indians replaced former slaves in the cane fields.
Natal’s planters turned to Indian indentured workers from 1860 when Africans would not accept plantation labour.
Walvin: the young Gandhi was radicalised by the mix of sugar, indenture and segregation in Natal.
Mintz: Palmerston’s ironies of 1841 belong to the debates that led to the equalisation of duties, and Walvin dates the abolition of British sugar duties to 1846.
Walvin: with the British duties gone in 1846, Cuba, already selling half its sugar to Britain, expanded to meet the demand.
Cuba’s rapid expansion rested on African labour that continued to arrive after British abolition.
Walvin: Cuban slavery was undermined by the war of 1868–78, in which slaves walked away.
Walvin: after the Ten Years’ War Spain reluctantly conceded, and Cuban slavery was abolished in 1886.
Walvin: with slavery ending, Cuban planters turned to indentured Chinese, over 150,000 by 1873.
Mazumdar: Guangdong exported labour to Cuba, Jamaica, Trinidad, Mauritius and Hawaii as well as sugar.
Walvin: Cuba made 750,000 tons in 1886, the year slavery ended there, and over a million tons by 1900.
Walvin: the US stake in Cuban sugar and the Sugar Trust’s refineries there are part of why sugar was ‘a decisive element’ in the 1898 war.
Walvin: the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 opened the delta to cane, which grew to 75 mills by 1812 and 1,536 estates by the Civil War.
Walvin: the Civil War laid waste the industry, cutting the plantations from 1,200 to 231 by 1864.
Walvin: the industry began a major recovery within a decade of the war, reaching 302,778 tons by 1900.
Walvin: missionaries on Kauai helped the first American sugar company of 1835, seeing the plantation as a means of conversion.
Walvin and Smith: the Reciprocity Treaty and Spreckels’s purchase transformed Hawaii’s sugar from 13,000 tons in 1876 to 105,000 in 1886.
The planters’ search for workers for the booming trade brought Japanese as well as Chinese labourers, by the thousands.
Walvin: Hawaii’s population had fallen below 60,000 by the 1870s, so the planters imported workers, and Japanese became the largest group.
Walvin and Smith: in 1887 the planters imposed a constitution securing control of the government.
Smith: the 1887 constitution was followed by the Marines’ overthrow of the monarchy in 1893 and annexation in 1898.
Walvin: Queensland’s planters relied on Melanesian labour, recruited by ‘blackbirding’ until 1904–06.
Mazumdar: the vacuum pan (1813) and the steam mill (1816) are the first steps of the same industrial revolution in cane sugar.
Mazumdar: the vacuum pan with the centrifuge cut the days of natural crystallisation to minutes.
Mazumdar: acid, charcoal and the centrifuge together allowed the standardised 95-degree product.
Mazumdar: steam mills’ advantage over oxen is shown by the Cuban comparison.
Mazumdar and Walvin: steam power and modern machinery underpinned Cuba’s growth.
Mazumdar: falling freight rates revolutionised the commodity market and with beet pushed prices down.
Walvin: the consolidation of British refining into a few large machine refineries went with rising consumption, from 30 lb in 1850 to 91 lb in 1914.
Walvin: working-class diets in the late nineteenth century came to rely on sugar — sweet tea, jam and bread.
Walvin links Keiller’s and Lipton’s jams to the new canning and bottling that fed the urban poor.
Walvin: canning and bottling, including the 1858 Mason jar, made preserving with sugar practicable.
Walvin: Americans’ rising consumption and the tariff made refining a monopoly of the Sugar Trust.
Walvin: new tariffs of 1890 kept Cuban raw sugar flowing into the east-coast refineries of the Trust.
Walvin: US protection began in 1842 and the McKinley Act of 1890 reset it.
Walvin: the soft-drink makers of the 1880s used sugar by the ton, in an American market consuming 80 lb a head by the 1890s.
Smith’s Quaker chocolate makers served the same expanding British market for sweets.
Graham’s warning came as American consumption grew from 5 lb a head in 1788 to 80 lb by the 1890s.
Walvin treats the doubling of world population as the main driver of the rising demand.
